import { getGitHubAppToken } from './auth';

export interface GitHubClientConfig {
  appId: string;
  installationId: string;
  privateKey: string;
}

/**
 * GitHub API client
 */
export class GitHubClient {
  private config: GitHubClientConfig;
  private tokenCache?: { token: string; expiresAt: number };

  constructor(config: GitHubClientConfig) {
    this.config = config;
  }

  /**
   * Get cached or fresh token
   */
  private async getToken(): Promise<string> {
    const now = Date.now() / 1000;
    if (this.tokenCache && this.tokenCache.expiresAt > now + 60) {
      return this.tokenCache.token;
    }

    const token = await getGitHubAppToken(
      this.config.appId,
      this.config.installationId,
      this.config.privateKey
    );

    this.tokenCache = {
      token,
      expiresAt: now + 55 * 60, // Tokens expire after 1 hour, cache for 55 min
    };

    return token;
  }

  /**
   * Make authenticated request to GitHub API
   */
  async request<T = any>(
    endpoint: string,
    options: RequestInit = {}
  ): Promise<T> {
    const token = await this.getToken();
    const url = `https://api.github.com${endpoint}`;

    const response = await fetch(url, {
      ...options,
      headers: {
        Authorization: `token ${token}`,
        Accept: 'application/vnd.github.v3+json',
        'User-Agent': 'Discord-GitHub-Bot',
        ...options.headers,
      },
    });

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`GitHub API error: ${response.status}`);
    }

    if (response.status === 204) {
      return null as any;
    }

    return response.json() as Promise<T>;
  }
}

/**
 * Simple helper for one-off requests (no caching)
 */
export async function githubRequest<T = any>(
  endpoint: string,
  config: GitHubClientConfig,
  options: RequestInit = {}
): Promise<T> {
  const token = await getGitHubAppToken(
    config.appId,
    config.installationId,
    config.privateKey
  );

  const url = `https://api.github.com${endpoint}`;

  const response = await fetch(url, {
    ...options,
    headers: {
      Authorization: `token ${token}`,
      Accept: 'application/vnd.github.v3+json',
      'User-Agent': 'Discord-GitHub-Bot',
      ...options.headers,
    },
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`GitHub API error: ${response.status}`);
  }

  if (response.status === 204) {
    return null as any;
  }

  return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}
export interface LinearClientConfig {
  apiKey: string;

/**
 * GraphQL response wrapper structure
 */
interface GraphQLResponse<T> {
  data?: T;
  errors?: Array<{
    message: string;
    locations?: Array<{ line: number; column: number }>;
    path?: Array<string | number>;
  }>;
}

/**
 * Linear API client using GraphQL
 */
export class LinearClient {
  private config: LinearClientConfig;

  constructor(config: LinearClientConfig) {
    this.config = config;
  }

  /**
   * Make authenticated GraphQL request to Linear API
   */
  async request<T>(
    query: string,
    variables?: Record<string, any>
  ): Promise<T> {
    const response = await fetch('https://api.linear.app/graphql', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: {
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        Authorization: this.config.apiKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({ query, variables }),
    });

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Linear API error: ${response.status}`);
    }

    const result = await response.json() as GraphQLResponse<T>;
    
    if (result.errors && result.errors.length > 0) {
      throw new Error(`Linear GraphQL error: ${result.errors[0].message}`);
    }
    
    if (!result.data) {
      throw new Error('Linear API returned no data');
    }

    return result.data;
  }
}

/**
 * Simple helper for one-off requests
 */
export async function linearRequest<T>(
  query: string,
  config: LinearClientConfig,
  variables?: Record<string, any>
): Promise<T> {
  const client = new LinearClient(config);
  return client.request<T>(query, variables);
}

export async function searchIssues(
  config: LinearClientConfig,
  teamId: string,
  searchQuery: string
) {
  const query = `
    query($teamId: String!, $filter: IssueFilter) {
      issues(filter: $filter, first: 25) {
        nodes {
          id
          identifier
          title
          description
          url
        }
      }
    }
  `;

  const result = await linearRequest<{
    issues: {
      nodes: Array<{
        id: string;
        identifier: string;
        title: string;
        description: string | null;
        url: string;
      }>;
    };
  }>(query, config, {
    teamId,
    filter: {
      team: { id: { eq: teamId } },
      or: [
        { title: { containsIgnoreCase: searchQuery } },
        { description: { containsIgnoreCase: searchQuery } },
      ],
    },
  });

  return result.issues.nodes;
}

) {

}

# AGENTS.md - AI Agent Development Guide for Superfunctions

> **Purpose**: This document provides AI agents with essential information for working effectively on the Superfunctions monorepo.

## 🏗️ Repository Structure

Superfunctions is a **Turbo monorepo** containing self-hosted developer tools and libraries. The repository is organized into:

### Core Functions (Top-Level Directories)

Individual superfunction packages, each providing specific developer capabilities:

- **`authfn/`** - Authentication & API key management
- **`cachefn/`** - Multi-tier caching with function memoization
- **`drawfn/`** - Cross-framework drawing canvas for brainstorming
- **`plugfn/`** - Integration platform (OAuth, webhooks, 75+ providers)
- **`searchfn/`** - Browser-first full-text search with IndexedDB
- **`secfn/`** - Security functions (secrets vault, rate limiting, monitoring)
- **`testfn/`** - Testing utilities and frameworks
- **`botfn/`** - Bot framework (Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations)
- **`hostfn/`** - Hosting and deployment utilities
- **`uifn/`** - UI components and utilities
- **`watchfn/`** - File watching and monitoring
- **`billfn/`** - Billing and payment processing
- **`browsefn/`** - Browser automation utilities
- **`chartfn/`** - Charting and visualization
- **`datafn/`** - Data processing utilities
- **`docsfn/`** - Documentation generation
- **`filefn/`** - File operations and management
- **`flowfn/`** - Flow control (queues, streams, workflows)
- **`iconfn/`** - Icon utilities
- **`logfn/`** - Logging utilities
- **`mailfn/`** - Programmable real inboxes for products, agents, and tests
- **`sendfn/`** - Email/messaging utilities

### Shared Packages (`packages/`)

Framework-agnostic core libraries used across superfunctions:

**TypeScript Packages:**

- `@superfunctions/http` - HTTP abstractions
- `@superfunctions/http-express` - Express.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-fastify` - Fastify adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-hono` - Hono adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-next` - Next.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-sveltekit` - SvelteKit adapter
- `@superfunctions/db` - Database adapter system (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- `@superfunctions/auth` - Authentication abstraction layer
- `@superfunctions/cli` - CLI tool for schema management

**Python Packages:**

- `superfunctions` (from `python-core/`) - Core namespace package
- `superfunctions-sqlalchemy` (from `python-sqlalchemy/`)
- `superfunctions-fastapi` (from `python-fastapi/`)
- `superfunctions-flask` (from `python-flask/`)

### Other Directories

- **`_conduct/`** - Root-level artifacts for shared code (implementation plans, specs, audits)
- **`21n/`** - Organization-specific packages
- **`.agent/`** - Agent workflows and automation
- **`.github/`** - GitHub Actions and CI/CD

## 📦 Package Naming Conventions

### Rule A: Shared Packages Format

**Any package shared across superfunctions uses `@superfunctions/{name}` format**

Examples:

```
packages/db/          → @superfunctions/db
packages/http/        → @superfunctions/http
packages/auth/        → @superfunctions/auth
packages/cli/         → @superfunctions/cli
```

### Rule B: Core Function Packages Format

**Single-package functions**: Use simple name without scope

```

- Don't reexport http-adapters etc - end consumers of the core function package will use the adapters directly. Refer `authfn` implementation for usage of core http router, core db, http adapters and db interface usage.
- Function packages that accept a `@superfunctions/db` `Adapter` must wrap the incoming adapter internally with their own schema, for example `wrapWithSchema(config.database, getSchema(...))`, before passing it to services/storage. Do not require app consumers to pass `adapterSchema` to `drizzleAdapter`, `kyselyAdapter`, `prismaAdapter`, or `memoryAdapter`; `adapterSchema` is a deprecated compatibility escape hatch for direct app-level adapter use.

### Code Organization

- Keep shared code in `packages/`
- Keep function-specific code in `{function}/`
- Use TypeScript for type safety
- Provide Python SDKs for backend-focused functions
- Write comprehensive tests

### Documentation

- Update README.md with usage examples
- Create SPEC.md for complex functions
- Document breaking changes
- Keep artifacts in `.conduct/` folders

### Testing

- Use Vitest for TypeScript
- Use pytest for Python
- Maintain high test coverage
- Test adapters separately

### Versioning

- Follow semantic versioning
- Coordinate versions across language SDKs
- Document migration guides for breaking changes

## 🔗 Related Resources

- **Repository**: https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions
- **License**: MIT (most packages) / Apache-2.0 (some packages)
- **Organization**: 21n
- **Contact**: hello@21n.org

## 📝 Notes for AI Agents

1. **Always check both TypeScript and Python** implementations when working on core functions
2. **Respect the naming conventions** - shared packages use `@superfunctions/`, functions use simple names
3. **Create artifacts in `.conduct/` folders**, not in root or arbitrary locations
4. **Avoid nested monorepos** - use subfolders within the main Turbo monorepo
5. **Use Turbo commands** for cross-package operations
6. **Check existing patterns** in similar functions before implementing new features
7. **Maintain consistency** across TypeScript and Python SDKs
8. **Update workspaces** in root `package.json` when adding new packages
9. **Follow existing test patterns** (Vitest for TS, pytest for Python)
10. **Document thoroughly** - this is a developer-focused ecosystem

---

**Package Manager**: npm@10.2.0
**Build Tool**: Turbo v2.0.0

# WatchFn core

Install `@watchfn/core` for collection, storage and the shared HTTP router. Framework integrations use explicit subpaths, so a core-only installation does not install Express, Fastify, Hono, Next.js or SvelteKit.

```ts
import { watchFn } from '@watchfn/core';

const watch = watchFn({ name: 'api', storage: 'memory', infra: { enabled: false } });
watch.start();
// Mount watch.httpRouter using the shared adapter for your framework.
// Before shutdown, await watch.stop() to finish admitted writes.
```

For Express, install `express` and `@superfunctions/http-express`. Mount the shared router with its adapter and import request tracking separately:

```ts
import express from 'express';
import { toExpress } from '@superfunctions/http-express';
import { createExpressMiddleware } from '@watchfn/core/adapters/express';

const app = express();
app.use(createExpressMiddleware(watch));
app.use('/watch', toExpress(watch.httpRouter));
```

Equivalent integration entry points are `@watchfn/core/adapters/fastify`, `/hono`, `/next`, and `/sveltekit`. Install the corresponding framework and `@superfunctions/http-<framework>` package when using that integration. Integration-specific router helpers remain available from these subpaths.

## Import migration

Framework helpers are no longer exported from the package root. Change, for example, `import { createExpressMiddleware } from '@watchfn/core'` to `import { createExpressMiddleware } from '@watchfn/core/adapters/express'`. Core imports such as `watchFn`, `WatchFn`, and `createWatchFnRouter` remain at the root. Both ESM and CommonJS runtime entry points are provided.

## Readiness limits

This is an ongoing readiness branch. Native provider, lifecycle, query aggregation and other original specification gates remain open. SvelteKit's currently resolved dependency graph has a low-severity `cookie` advisory with no automatic npm fix. Keeping that integration optional avoids installing it for unrelated core consumers; it does not remediate the SvelteKit-specific advisory.

## Canonical bug reports and BotFn issues

Opt in with `botfn` to transactionally persist canonical CatchFn/WatchFn `bug_report` events with a delivery outbox. Use a durable shared DB adapter with transactions, configure an ingestion API key, and migrate both `getWatchFnSchema()` and `getBugIssueSchema()` before enabling intake. WatchFn wraps the incoming adapter with those schemas internally; do not pass `adapterSchema` yourself.

This is **one trusted application/API-key boundary**. Every holder of the configured Watch API key can choose any configured app route and query all stored events. `namespace` separates outbox identities, claims and status; it does not provide tenant isolation for Watch's existing query API. Use separate deployments and databases for mutually untrusted tenants.

```ts
import { WatchFn, getWatchFnSchema, getBugIssueSchema } from '@watchfn/core';
import { GitHubClient } from '@botfn/github-integration';

// Apply your database migration using this combined schema before accepting traffic.
const schema = { ...getWatchFnSchema(), ...getBugIssueSchema() };
const watch = new WatchFn({
  name: 'checkout', storage: 'database', database,
  auth: { apiKey: process.env.WATCH_INGEST_KEY! },
  botfn: {
    namespace: 'checkout-production',
    routes: [{ app: 'checkout', target: 'github', project: 'acme/bugs',
      client: new GitHubClient({ appId, installationId, privateKey }) }],
  },
});
watch.start();
// Mount watch.httpRouter with the shared HTTP adapter. Schedule this on the server:
await watch.processBugIssues(20);
const status = await watch.getBugIssueStatus({ app: 'checkout', reportId });
// An operator may recover an ambiguous create only by verifying the existing issue:
await watch.reconcileBugIssue({ app: 'checkout', reportId }, '123');
await watch.stop();
```

A Linear route uses `target: 'linear'`, `project: teamId`, and BotFn's `LinearClient`. The existing BotFn packages expose TypeScript source; use the repository build/runtime configuration that supports those clients. No BotFn provider credential or request-client object is persisted by WatchFn.

Clients may send `integration: { target: 'github', project: 'acme/bugs' }` only to select a matching server route. With one matching route, the hint is optional. Client-supplied `issueId`/`issueUrl` are rejected when this integration is enabled. HTTP 202 means canonical event and pending delivery state are committed, **not that an issue already exists**. Same namespace/app/report ID and identical content deduplicates; changed content returns 409. Each report is its own transaction: a later failure in a batch can follow earlier committed reports. Retry canonical reports with their original IDs and content.

Delivery claims use database CAS and leases. A failed, timed-out, expired or malformed create outcome enters `reconciliation` and is never automatically created again. The privileged server reconciliation method reads the selected issue from the configured provider and verifies repository/team, report marker, issue ID and allowed HTTPS URL before atomically linking it back into the canonical event. Do not expose these server methods without your own operator authorization. Querying the canonical event after linkage returns its `integration.issueId` and `integration.issueUrl`.

Scheduling and migration remain the host's responsibility. `processBugIssues` examines at most 1–100 candidates per call (default 20); repeat calls to drain the queue and recover expired leases. `stop()` waits for already admitted work; it does not automatically process pending reports. The default provider wait is 10 seconds and lease is 30 seconds. Linear's existing client does not accept an abort signal, and existing BotFn clients parse full provider JSON: a timeout bounds worker waiting, not all network activity or provider-response memory. Unknown remote side effects require operator reconciliation. See [the migration, acceptance and remaining limits](../.conduct/botfn-issue-readiness.md).
EOF
cat > ../.conduct/botfn-issue-readiness.md <<'EOF'
# Canonical bug intake and BotFn issue delivery

The original CatchFn issue-sync path now uses WatchFn's canonical `bug_report` intake, shared HTTP router and internally schema-wrapped shared DB. This is opt-in prospective issue delivery, not the separate flat CatchFn report service.

## Contract and migration

Use one trusted application boundary per deployment. The existing Watch API key authorizes all configured app routes and all Watch queries. Routes are server-owned destination allowlists, not per-key app authorization. Outbox namespace scopes report identities and delivery methods, not tenant-isolated query reads. Mutually untrusted tenants require separate deployments/databases. Browser/Catch clients receive only an ingestion credential, never provider credentials; deployment must decide whether exposing that ingestion credential suits its trust boundary.

Before enabling `botfn`, apply an additive migration for `getBugIssueSchema()` alongside `getWatchFnSchema()`. The new `watchfn_bug_issues` table has a unique ID derived from namespace/app/report ID, immutable fingerprint, event reference, trusted route identity, status/revision/lease, timestamps, attempt count and verified linkage. Its queue index covers namespace/state/id. Existing event schema/data is unchanged. Missing schema causes intake failure (503), not successful delivery. Transaction capability is required; no adapter name is treated as proof of physical durability. The built-in memory/legacy event stores cannot enable this integration. Shared memory adapters remain useful for contract tests only; hosts are responsible for using a durable configured provider.

Only newly submitted canonical reports are queued. Existing generic-arrival event rows are not silently backfilled or rewritten, and their old IDs are not retrospectively deduplicated. Stop old writers before switching a deployment; choose a stable namespace and preserve new canonical IDs/content across retries. Do not replay historical reports into an enabled integration unless creating their issue is intended. Disabling the integration returns to legacy generic-arrival storage semantics; it does not process existing outbox rows. Keep a delivery-enabled worker configured until its queue is resolved, and do not mix enabled/disabled writers if replay deduplication is required.

The immutable fingerprint is computed from the original JSON envelope. Successful linkage changes only the stored event's integration fields; replaying the original envelope remains a deduplicated acknowledgment. An altered report with the same namespace/app/ID returns 409. All request routes are validated before any batch writes, but each report commits separately: later storage/conflict failures can follow earlier commits. Non-bug events retain their original arrival semantics and are not made idempotent by this feature.

A transaction commits event plus pending outbox before HTTP 202. Explicit server worker calls claim candidates with revision CAS and unique leases. Missing route/event fails before the provider call with an explicit failure code. ## Canonical bug reports and BotFn issues

Opt in with `botfn` to transactionally persist canonical CatchFn/WatchFn `bug_report` events with a delivery outbox. Use a durable shared DB adapter with transactions, configure an ingestion API key, and migrate both `getWatchFnSchema()` and `getBugIssueSchema()` before enabling intake. import { GitHubClient } from '@botfn/github-integration';

// Apply your database migration using this combined schema before accepting traffic.
const schema = { ...getWatchFnSchema(), ...getBugIssueSchema() };
const watch = new WatchFn({
  name: 'checkout', storage: 'database', database,
  auth: { apiKey: process.env.WATCH_INGEST_KEY! },
  botfn: {
    namespace: 'checkout-production',
    routes: [{ app: 'checkout', target: 'github', project: 'acme/bugs',
      client: new GitHubClient({ appId, installationId, privateKey }) }],
  },
});
watch.start();
// Mount watch.httpRouter with the shared HTTP adapter. Schedule this on the server:
await watch.processBugIssues(20);
const status = await watch.getBugIssueStatus({ app: 'checkout', reportId });
// An operator may recover an ambiguous create only by verifying the existing issue:
await watch.reconcileBugIssue({ app: 'checkout', reportId }, '123');
await watch.stop();

A Linear route uses `target: 'linear'`, `project: teamId`, and BotFn's `LinearClient`. The existing BotFn packages expose TypeScript source; use the repository build/runtime configuration that supports those clients. No BotFn provider credential or request-client object is persisted by WatchFn.

Clients may send `integration: { target: 'github', project: 'acme/bugs' }` only to select a matching server route. With one matching route, the hint is optional. Client-supplied `issueId`/`issueUrl` are rejected when this integration is enabled. HTTP 202 means canonical event and pending delivery state are committed, **not that an issue already exists**. Same namespace/app/report ID and identical content deduplicates; changed content returns 409. Each report is its own transaction: a later failure in a batch can follow earlier committed reports. Retry canonical reports with their original IDs and content.

Delivery claims use database CAS and leases. A failed, timed-out, expired or malformed create outcome enters `reconciliation` and is never automatically created again. The privileged server reconciliation method reads the selected issue from the configured provider and verifies repository/team, report marker, issue ID and allowed HTTPS URL before atomically linking it back into the canonical event. ## Server-side GitHub/Linear issue delivery

The canonical WatchFn endpoint can enable its transactional BotFn issue outbox. CatchFn supplies only a routing hint; configure provider clients, tokens/private keys, allowed repositories/teams and the durable database on the Watch server.

```ts
const catcher = catchFn({
  name: 'shop',
  watch: { endpoint: '/watch/ingest', apiKey: watchApiKey },
  integration: { target: 'github', project: 'acme/bugs' },
});
const report = await catcher.captureBug({
  title: 'Checkout failed',
  // Optional per-report override, restricted by the Watch server's route allowlist:
  integration: { target: 'linear', project: 'team-id' },
});
```

The hint is optional when the server can select one route for the app. Invalid hints and provider-credential fields are rejected locally; unauthorized destinations are rejected by WatchFn. A provider issue ID or URL is a server result, not a client routing input.

`report.delivery === 'sent'` means the canonical report and pending issue delivery were acknowledged by WatchFn. It does not mean the provider issue already exists. Watch's explicit server worker creates the issue; the linked canonical event then exposes `integration.issueId`/`issueUrl` through its authenticated query API. The reporter still displays an issue link when an injected client returns one, but automatic refresh of a later asynchronous issue link is not implemented. Do not fabricate a provider link from a successful HTTP202.

The configured Watch API key also authorizes Watch queries and every configured route; there is no ingestion-only key or per-app credential isolation in this integration. Use an authenticated application-backend proxy when exposing that key in the browser is unsuitable. All apps sharing one Watch deployment/key must share its trust boundary. Provider credentials remain server-only.

Enabled outbox intake deduplicates the same canonical report ID/content, including a lost acknowledgment retried by the shared Watch browser transport. Modified content for an existing ID returns409. The existing `CatchFnDeliveryError.retry()` retains the original report for retry; calling `captureBug()` again creates a new report. WatchFn without the outbox retains its original at-least-once arrival behavior.

See [BotFn delivery acceptance and limits](../.conduct/botfn-delivery-readiness.md) and [WatchFn migration/worker setup](../../watchfn/.conduct/botfn-issue-readiness.md).
EOF

# Canonical CatchFn to BotFn issue delivery

This checkpoint connects the original canonical CatchFn bug-report path to WatchFn's transactional issue outbox and actual BotFn provider clients. It does not route through the separate flat-report persistence service.

## Client and server contract

`CatchFnConfig.integration` supplies an optional default `{target?, project?}` hint; `captureBug({integration})` overrides it per report. The event and canonical envelope retain that hint. The server chooses only a configured app/target/project route. Client options reject unsupported target values, empty/oversized projects, arbitrary extra fields and provider credentials. Provider keys and clients belong only in WatchFn server configuration. Server linkage fields remain supported on returned reports from an injected client, but are not accepted as creation hints.

A202 acknowledgment means the canonical event and outbox entry are committed, not that a provider issue exists. Delivery is explicit server work. Exact replay under the enabled outbox deduplicates by namespace/app/report ID and immutable content; modified content conflicts. Original retry closures retain the ID/envelope. Without this opt-in Watch integration, existing generic arrival semantics remain at least once.

The Watch API key authorizes both ingestion and query and every route in its deployment. This is one trusted application boundary, not per-app/tenant authorization. Use an authenticated app-backend proxy if the full Watch key is unsuitable for browser exposure. Outbox namespaces do not make Watch queries tenant-isolated. Provider credentials stay server-side. Privileged delivery/status/reconciliation methods require host/operator access control if exposed remotely.

The TypeScript browser SDK is the canonical client described by this original specification. Existing Python code is the separate flat-report server contract, not a canonical Watch transport SDK; it remains unchanged and does not gain or claim BotFn delivery from this change.

## Validation

- CatchFn TypeScript SDK:92 tests across9 files pass, including default/override hint preservation, no false issue acknowledgment and malformed/credential-hint rejection. Source typecheck and dual-format/declaration build pass.
- `node catchfn/typescript/scripts/botfn-acceptance.mjs` passes using the built Catch SDK, actual shared Watch browser transport, built Watch core, real loopback HTTP, actual native SQLite and the actual BotFn GitHub client bundled from source. An ordinary PKCS#1 RSA PEM produces a verified JWT for an installation-token request before issue creation.
- The same acceptance launches installed Chrome and submits through the actual browser CatchFn SDK into Watch HTTP. It verifies pending acknowledgment without an invented link, authenticated routing, server delivery and persisted provider linkage.
- A dropped intake response triggers identical canonical replay and stores exactly one event/outbox. Pending state survives database close/reopen before delivery. Both Node and browser reports retain linkage across another close/reopen. Wrong API keys and unconfigured repository hints fail; redacted context persists without being included in provider issue text. Reprocessing linked rows sends no additional creates.
- Watch's separate native acceptance covers both actual GitHub and Linear request clients, two-connection claims, transaction rollback, lost provider response and verified reconciliation after reopening. See `watchfn/.conduct/botfn-issue-readiness.md` for exact scope.

Reproduction requires built shared DB, Watch browser/core and Catch SDK plus local `better-sqlite3`, `kysely`, esbuild, Playwright and Chrome. The acceptance script supports `CATCHFN_WATCH_CORE=/absolute/path/to/dist/index.mjs`. This run used the built Watch artifact from the identical merged Watch commit in the sibling readiness checkout: the Catch tree's intentionally scoped install lacks optional HTTP-adapter packages required by the full Watch multi-entry build. Catch's own SDK builds/types pass; the full Watch build and fresh packed matrix were validated in its own checkout. No dependency or lockfile changes were needed.

## Remaining original gates

No hosted issue or message was created. Local protocol fixtures exercise real clients and authentication code, not live GitHub installation permissions, Linear workspace access or provider reliability. The original hosted-provider acceptance, per-tenant query/auth design, scalable event query indexing, production worker/retention operations, BotFn package deployment and v1.1 closed-issue synchronization remain open.

The reporter can show a link returned immediately by an injected client, but does not automatically poll for a link created later by the outbox worker. Application-specific status UI/authorized polling remains open. Linear's current request interface cannot cancel the underlying operation and both existing provider clients parse full response JSON; Watch's wait timeout is not a universal transport/memory bound. Unknown provider outcomes are parked for verified operator reconciliation and are never automatically recreated. This is a tested canonical integration checkpoint, not full CatchFn/WatchFn/BotFn readiness.
EOF

{"cmd":"cat > watchfn/.conduct/issue-status-readiness.md <<'EOF'
# Bounded issue-status reads

`POST /issues/status` is a read-only companion to canonical bug intake. It uses the same configured Watch API-key authority as ingestion/query; it does not provide an ingestion-only key, per-app authorization, operator reconciliation or any mutation. The request is a strict `{app,reportId}` object capped at4KiB; invalid input returns400/413, unauthorized input401 before body parsing, absent records404, and unavailable integration/storage503. Successful no-store responses expose only app/report, target, state and verified linkage, with a16KiB serialized ceiling. Provider destination and URL checks remain enforced before linked status is returned.

`BrowserClient.readBugIssueStatus(reference,{signal})` performs one authenticated request without queue mutation or automatic retry. It derives `/mount/issues/status` only from an exact `/mount/ingest` URL with no query/hash; other ingestion routes require explicit `issueStatusEndpoint`. Relative URLs resolve against browser location. Existing dynamic headers/API keys are reused. The method caps streamed response bytes at16KiB, validates reference binding and state/link coherence, and accepts linked HTTPS GitHub/Linear issue URLs only for the returned target. It rejects redirects, malformed replies and dangerous links. Missing records return null; authorization/unavailability failures remain errors.

Timeout covers fetch and body consumption even if a custom fetch ignores AbortSignal. External abort and client close reject outstanding reads promptly; late responses are canceled/ignored. This bounds waiting and retained response bytes, not transport behavior under a noncompliant fetch implementation. The same full Watch key authorizes all routes and queries: use an authorized application-backend proxy if browser exposure is unsuitable.

Validation: three focused core HTTP tests cover strict/authenticated bounded requests, absence/pending/linked states, no-store responses, reference separation and disabled integration. Thirteen browser tests cover mounted endpoint derivation, explicit override, refreshed authentication, absence/errors, forged or unsafe receipts, byte limits, timeout, close and ignored-signal cancellation. Full browser suite28 tests and its CJS/ESM/IIFE/declaration build pass; core source typecheck passes. Full core and package-consumer checks accompany the checkpoint. Hosted providers and the broader original readiness gates remain open.
EOF
cat >> watchfn/typescript/README.md <<'EOF'

Authenticated clients can read `POST /issues/status` with `{app,reportId}` to obtain pending/processing/reconciliation/linked state and verified provider linkage. It returns404 for an absent report and503 if issue integration is unavailable. This read-only route uses the same full Watch API key as ingestion and query; it does not expose operator reconciliation. The browser package's `readBugIssueStatus` derives `/mount/issues/status` from `/mount/ingest`, or accepts an explicit `issueStatusEndpoint` for custom routes. Reads are bounded and cancelable; see [status-read behavior](../.conduct/issue-status-readiness.md).

"""Framework-neutral route middleware execution."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any, Awaitable, Callable, Optional, cast

from .types import Response, Route, RouteContext


async def execute_route(
    route: Optional[Route],
    handler: Callable[..., Awaitable[Response]],
    request: Any,
    context: RouteContext,
) -> Response:
    """Execute route middleware in declaration order, then the handler."""
    next_handler: Callable[..., Awaitable[Response]] = handler
    for middleware in reversed((route.middleware or []) if route else []):
        downstream = next_handler

        async def invoke(
            current_request: Any,
            current_context: RouteContext,
            middleware: Any = middleware,
            downstream: Callable[..., Awaitable[Response]] = downstream,
        ) -> Response:
            return cast(
                Response,
                await middleware(current_request, current_context, downstream),
            )

        next_handler = invoke
    return cast(Response, await next_handler(request, context))

# CatchFn Specification (Draft)

Last updated: 2026-01-14  
Status: Draft (implementation not started)  
Owner: Platform (Superfunctions)

## Goal
Create `catchfn`, a self-hosted bug capture and reporting layer (similar to Bugasura/Jam.dev) built on top of existing Superfunctions primitives. Focus on lightweight in-app reporting, automated context capture, issue syncing, and reuse of `watchfn` for ingestion/analysis.

## Scope (v1)
- In-app reporter widget (JS/browser) that lets users submit a bug with screenshot/annotation, description, steps, severity, tags.
- Automatic context capture: URL, user/session, environment, console logs, network requests summary, breadcrumbs, device info.
- Manual API: `catchFn().captureBug()` to programmatically submit bug reports.
- Storage/transport: reuse `watchfn` ingestion/event router; introduce `bug_report` event type.
- Issue sync: optional auto-create/link to GitHub/Linear via existing `botfn` integrations.
- Attachments: inline screenshot (base64 or blob reference) and optional additional attachments (URLs or uploaded via `watchfn` file channel if available).

## Persistence & Storage
- Transport: reuse `watchfn` ingestion endpoint/auth/batching; no new transport surface.
- Schema: extend `watchfn` event schema with `type: "bug_report"` and the data model above; validate required fields at ingest.
- Storage: same datastore as other watchfn events; partition by `app`/`type`; indexes on (`type`, `app`, `timestamp`), (`type`, `app`, `report.severity`), (`integration.issueId`), (`sessionId`), (`replayId`).
- Attachments: small images inline (data URL); large assets uploaded via watchfn’s file channel/blob adapter and stored as URLs in the event record.
- Query: accessible via watchfn query API with filters for `type = bug_report`, severity, tags, time range, app.
- Retention: default to watchfn retention; allow `bug_report`-specific TTL override and size caps (truncate console/network logs to last N).

## Non-Goals (v1)
- Full dashboard UI (rely on `watchfn` queries/filters for now).
- Native mobile SDKs (web-only; React Native later).
- Video/session replay (planned v1.1).
- On-prem deployment changes (reuse existing `watchfn` deployment).

## Personas & Use Cases
- Frontend engineers: fast repro context when a user reports an issue.
- QA: submit annotated repros during test runs; auto-file to GitHub/Linear.
- Support: capture user-facing issues with environment + logs without dev tools.

## Architecture
- Client SDK (`catchfn/typescript/src`):
  - Wraps/depends on `watchfn` browser client for transport and breadcrumbs.
  - Reporter widget UI (vanilla + React helper) that triggers capture + UI overlay.
  - Uses `drawfn` for screenshot annotation.
- Event model:
  - New event type `bug_report` in `watchfn` ingestion schema.
  - Stored alongside other watch events; query via `watchfn` API.
- Issue sync:
  - Optional webhook/bridge to `botfn` persistence service to create/link issues (GitHub/Linear).
  - Status sync via existing `botfn` jobs/hooks.
- Session replay (v1.1):
  - Plugin that records DOM mutations/redacted inputs; links `replayId` to bug report.

"""Framework-neutral route middleware execution."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any, Awaitable, Callable, Optional, cast

from .types import Response, Route, RouteContext


async def execute_route(
    route: Optional[Route],
    handler: Callable[..., Awaitable[Response]],
    request: Any,
    context: RouteContext,
) -> Response:
    """Execute route middleware in declaration order, then the handler."""
    next_handler: Callable[..., Awaitable[Response]] = handler
    for middleware in reversed((route.middleware or []) if route else []):
        downstream = next_handler

        async def invoke(
            current_request: Any,
            current_context: RouteContext,
            middleware: Any = middleware,
            downstream: Callable[..., Awaitable[Response]] = downstream,
        ) -> Response:
            return cast(
                Response,
                await middleware(current_request, current_context, downstream),
            )

        next_handler = invoke
    return cast(Response, await next_handler(request, context))

## Goal
Create `catchfn`, a self-hosted bug capture and reporting layer (similar to Bugasura/Jam.dev) built on top of existing Superfunctions primitives. Focus on lightweight in-app reporting, automated context capture, issue syncing, and reuse of `watchfn` for ingestion/analysis.

## Scope (v1)
- In-app reporter widget (JS/browser) that lets users submit a bug with screenshot/annotation, description, steps, severity, tags.
- Automatic context capture: URL, user/session, environment, console logs, network requests summary, breadcrumbs, device info.
- Manual API: `catchFn().captureBug()` to programmatically submit bug reports.
- Storage/transport: reuse `watchfn` ingestion/event router; introduce `bug_report` event type.
- Issue sync: optional auto-create/link to GitHub/Linear via existing `botfn` integrations.
- Attachments: inline screenshot (base64 or blob reference) and optional additional attachments (URLs or uploaded via `watchfn` file channel if available).

## Persistence & Storage
- Transport: reuse `watchfn` ingestion endpoint/auth/batching; no new transport surface.
- Schema: extend `watchfn` event schema with `type: "bug_report"` and the data model above; validate required fields at ingest.
- Storage: same datastore as other watchfn events; partition by `app`/`type`; indexes on (`type`, `app`, `timestamp`), (`type`, `app`, `report.severity`), (`integration.issueId`), (`sessionId`), (`replayId`).
- Attachments: small images inline (data URL); large assets uploaded via watchfn’s file channel/blob adapter and stored as URLs in the event record.
- Query: accessible via watchfn query API with filters for `type = bug_report`, severity, tags, time range, app.
- Retention: default to watchfn retention; allow `bug_report`-specific TTL override and size caps (truncate console/network logs to last N).

## Non-Goals (v1)
- Full dashboard UI (rely on `watchfn` queries/filters for now).
- Native mobile SDKs (web-only; React Native later).
- Video/session replay (planned v1.1).
- On-prem deployment changes (reuse existing `watchfn` deployment).

## Personas & Use Cases
- Frontend engineers: fast repro context when a user reports an issue.
- QA: submit annotated repros during test runs; auto-file to GitHub/Linear.
- Support: capture user-facing issues with environment + logs without dev tools.

- Client SDK (`catchfn/typescript/src`):
  - Wraps/depends on `watchfn` browser client for transport and breadcrumbs.
  - Reporter widget UI (vanilla + React helper) that triggers capture + UI overlay.
  - Uses `drawfn` for screenshot annotation.
- Event model:
  - New event type `bug_report` in `watchfn` ingestion schema.
  - Stored alongside other watch events; query via `watchfn` API.
- Issue sync:
  - Optional webhook/bridge to `botfn` persistence service to create/link issues (GitHub/Linear).
  - Status sync via existing `botfn` jobs/hooks.
- Session replay (v1.1):
  - Plugin that records DOM mutations/redacted inputs; links `replayId` to bug report.

# AGENTS.md - AI Agent Development Guide for Superfunctions

> **Purpose**: This document provides AI agents with essential information for working effectively on the Superfunctions monorepo.

## 🏗️ Repository Structure

Superfunctions is a **Turbo monorepo** containing self-hosted developer tools and libraries. The repository is organized into:

### Core Functions (Top-Level Directories)

Individual superfunction packages, each providing specific developer capabilities:

- **`authfn/`** - Authentication & API key management
- **`cachefn/`** - Multi-tier caching with function memoization
- **`drawfn/`** - Cross-framework drawing canvas for brainstorming
- **`plugfn/`** - Integration platform (OAuth, webhooks, 75+ providers)
- **`searchfn/`** - Browser-first full-text search with IndexedDB
- **`secfn/`** - Security functions (secrets vault, rate limiting, monitoring)
- **`testfn/`** - Testing utilities and frameworks
- **`botfn/`** - Bot framework (Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations)
- **`hostfn/`** - Hosting and deployment utilities
- **`uifn/`** - UI components and utilities
- **`watchfn/`** - File watching and monitoring
- **`billfn/`** - Billing and payment processing
- **`browsefn/`** - Browser automation utilities
- **`chartfn/`** - Charting and visualization
- **`datafn/`** - Data processing utilities
- **`docsfn/`** - Documentation generation
- **`filefn/`** - File operations and management
- **`flowfn/`** - Flow control (queues, streams, workflows)
- **`iconfn/`** - Icon utilities
- **`logfn/`** - Logging utilities
- **`mailfn/`** - Programmable real inboxes for products, agents, and tests
- **`sendfn/`** - Email/messaging utilities

### Shared Packages (`packages/`)

Framework-agnostic core libraries used across superfunctions:

**TypeScript Packages:**

- `@superfunctions/http` - HTTP abstractions
- `@superfunctions/http-express` - Express.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-fastify` - Fastify adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-hono` - Hono adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-next` - Next.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-sveltekit` - SvelteKit adapter
- `@superfunctions/db` - Database adapter system (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- `@superfunctions/auth` - Authentication abstraction layer
- `@superfunctions/cli` - CLI tool for schema management

**Python Packages:**

- `superfunctions` (from `python-core/`) - Core namespace package
- `superfunctions-sqlalchemy` (from `python-sqlalchemy/`)
- `superfunctions-fastapi` (from `python-fastapi/`)
- `superfunctions-flask` (from `python-flask/`)

### Other Directories

- **`_conduct/`** - Root-level artifacts for shared code (implementation plans, specs, audits)
- **`21n/`** - Organization-specific packages
- **`.agent/`** - Agent workflows and automation
- **`.github/`** - GitHub Actions and CI/CD

## 📦 Package Naming Conventions

### Rule A: Shared Packages Format

**Any package shared across superfunctions uses `@superfunctions/{name}` format**

Examples:

```
packages/db/          → @superfunctions/db
packages/http/        → @superfunctions/http
packages/auth/        → @superfunctions/auth
packages/cli/         → @superfunctions/cli
```

### Rule B: Core Function Packages Format

**Single-package functions**: Use simple name without scope

```
authfn/ts-sdk/        → authfn
drawfn/core/          → drawfn
cachefn/typescript/   → cachefn
plugfn/core/         → plugfn
searchfn/             → searchfn
```

**Multi-package functions**: Use `@{functionname}/{sub-package}` format (if needed in future)

```
@authfn/core          (example for future multi-package structure)
@authfn/providers     (example for future multi-package structure)
```

**Current Status**: All core functions currently use single-package structure. The scoped format is reserved for future expansion if a function needs multiple published packages.

### Rule C: Monorepo Structure

**The root `superfunctions` is a Turbo monorepo. Avoid nested monorepos.**

- ✅ Use subfolders to organize functions (e.g., `authfn/python/`, `authfn/ts-sdk/`)
- ❌ Do NOT create nested monorepos (e.g., `authfn/` should NOT be another monorepo)
- ✅ Use Turbo workspaces defined in root `package.json`

Current workspaces:

```json
{
  "workspaces": [
    "searchfn",
    "botfn/*",
    "hostfn/*",
    "authfn/*",
    "packages/*",
    "21n/*"
  ]
}
```

### Rule D: Artifact Location

**Create artifacts (`.md` files) in `.conduct` folders**

- **Function-specific artifacts**: `{function}/.conduct/`
  - Examples: `authfn/.conduct/implementation.md`, `drawfn/.conduct/audit_report.md`
- **Shared/root artifacts**: `_conduct/`
  - Examples: `_conduct/implementation.md`, `_conduct/spec.md`

Artifact types:

- `implementation.md` - Implementation plans
- `spec.md` - Technical specifications
- `audit_report.md` - Code audits and reviews
- `task.md` - Task tracking
- `walkthrough.md` - Feature walkthroughs

## 🗂️ Language Support

Most core functions support **both TypeScript and Python**:

### TypeScript Structure

```
{function}/
├── typescript/       or  core/
│   ├── src/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── tsconfig.json
│   └── vitest.config.ts
```

### Python Structure

```
{function}/
├── python/
│   ├── {function}/        # Python package directory
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── tests/
│   ├── pyproject.toml
│   └── README.md
```

### Examples

- `authfn/typescript/` + `authfn/python/`
- `cachefn/typescript/` + `cachefn/python/`
- `secfn/typescript/` + `secfn/python/`
- `plugfn/core/` + `plugfn/python/`
- `drawfn/core/` (TypeScript only, with React/Svelte adapters)
- `searchfn/` (TypeScript only, browser-focused)

### Building

```bash
# Build all packages
npm run build

# Build specific package (from root)
turbo run build --filter=authfn
turbo run build --filter=@superfunctions/db

# Build from package directory
cd authfn/ts-sdk && npm run build
```

### Testing

```bash
# Test all packages
npm test

# Test specific package
turbo run test --filter=drawfn

# Watch mode
npm run test:watch
```

### Linting

```bash
npm run lint
```

### Package Manager

- **npm** (v10.2.0+) - Specified in `packageManager` field
- Uses npm workspaces for monorepo management
- Turbo for build orchestration

## 🎯 Key Superfunctions Features

### AuthFn

- Multi-provider authentication (OAuth, API keys, JWT)
- Framework-agnostic with adapters for Express, Fastify, Hono, Next.js, SvelteKit
- Database-agnostic (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- TypeScript + Python SDKs

- React and Svelte adapters
- Scene management, export capabilities

- Webhook support
- Multi-tenant with secure token storage

- BM25 scoring

- Function memoization

- Browser and server support

- Secrets vault management
- Access control and permissions
- Rate limiting

- Secret scanning

### BotFn

- Multi-platform bot framework
- Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations
- Shared types and persistence layer
- Event-driven architecture

## 🛠️ Common Tasks

### Adding a New Function

1. Create top-level directory: `{functionname}/`
2. Add TypeScript SDK: `{functionname}/typescript/` or `{functionname}/ts-sdk/`
3. (Optional) Add Python SDK: `{functionname}/python/`
4. Create `.conduct/` for artifacts
5. Add to workspace in root `package.json`
6. Package name: `{functionname}` (not scoped unless multi-package)

### Adding a Shared Package

1. Create in `packages/{name}/`
2. Package name: `@superfunctions/{name}`
3. Add to workspace (already covered by `packages/*`)
4. Update dependent packages

### Creating Artifacts

1. Function-specific: `{function}/.conduct/{artifact}.md`
2. Shared/root: `_conduct/{artifact}.md`
3. Use consistent naming: `implementation.md`, `spec.md`, `audit_report.md`, etc.

```bash
# Run task across all packages
turbo run build
turbo run test

turbo run build --filter=authfn

- Function packages that accept a `@superfunctions/db` `Adapter` must wrap the incoming adapter internally with their own schema, for example `wrapWithSchema(config.database, getSchema(...))`, before passing it to services/storage. # AGENTS.md - AI Agent Development Guide for Superfunctions

> **Purpose**: This document provides AI agents with essential information for working effectively on the Superfunctions monorepo.

## 🏗️ Repository Structure

Superfunctions is a **Turbo monorepo** containing self-hosted developer tools and libraries. The repository is organized into:

### Core Functions (Top-Level Directories)

Individual superfunction packages, each providing specific developer capabilities:

- **`authfn/`** - Authentication & API key management
- **`cachefn/`** - Multi-tier caching with function memoization
- **`drawfn/`** - Cross-framework drawing canvas for brainstorming
- **`plugfn/`** - Integration platform (OAuth, webhooks, 75+ providers)
- **`searchfn/`** - Browser-first full-text search with IndexedDB
- **`secfn/`** - Security functions (secrets vault, rate limiting, monitoring)
- **`testfn/`** - Testing utilities and frameworks
- **`botfn/`** - Bot framework (Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations)
- **`hostfn/`** - Hosting and deployment utilities
- **`uifn/`** - UI components and utilities
- **`watchfn/`** - File watching and monitoring
- **`billfn/`** - Billing and payment processing
- **`browsefn/`** - Browser automation utilities
- **`chartfn/`** - Charting and visualization
- **`datafn/`** - Data processing utilities
- **`docsfn/`** - Documentation generation
- **`filefn/`** - File operations and management
- **`flowfn/`** - Flow control (queues, streams, workflows)
- **`iconfn/`** - Icon utilities
- **`logfn/`** - Logging utilities
- **`mailfn/`** - Programmable real inboxes for products, agents, and tests
- **`sendfn/`** - Email/messaging utilities

### Shared Packages (`packages/`)

Framework-agnostic core libraries used across superfunctions:

**TypeScript Packages:**

- `@superfunctions/http` - HTTP abstractions
- `@superfunctions/http-express` - Express.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-fastify` - Fastify adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-hono` - Hono adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-next` - Next.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-sveltekit` - SvelteKit adapter
- `@superfunctions/db` - Database adapter system (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- `@superfunctions/auth` - Authentication abstraction layer
- `@superfunctions/cli` - CLI tool for schema management

**Python Packages:**

- `superfunctions` (from `python-core/`) - Core namespace package
- `superfunctions-sqlalchemy` (from `python-sqlalchemy/`)
- `superfunctions-fastapi` (from `python-fastapi/`)
- `superfunctions-flask` (from `python-flask/`)

### Other Directories

- **`_conduct/`** - Root-level artifacts for shared code (implementation plans, specs, audits)
- **`21n/`** - Organization-specific packages
- **`.agent/`** - Agent workflows and automation
- **`.github/`** - GitHub Actions and CI/CD

## 📦 Package Naming Conventions

### Rule A: Shared Packages Format

**Any package shared across superfunctions uses `@superfunctions/{name}` format**

Examples:

```
packages/db/          → @superfunctions/db
packages/http/        → @superfunctions/http
packages/auth/        → @superfunctions/auth
packages/cli/         → @superfunctions/cli
```

### Rule B: Core Function Packages Format

**Single-package functions**: Use simple name without scope

```
authfn/ts-sdk/        → authfn
drawfn/core/          → drawfn
cachefn/typescript/   → cachefn
plugfn/core/         → plugfn
searchfn/             → searchfn
```

**Multi-package functions**: Use `@{functionname}/{sub-package}` format (if needed in future)

```
@authfn/core          (example for future multi-package structure)
@authfn/providers     (example for future multi-package structure)
```

**Current Status**: All core functions currently use single-package structure. The scoped format is reserved for future expansion if a function needs multiple published packages.

### Rule C: Monorepo Structure

**The root `superfunctions` is a Turbo monorepo. Avoid nested monorepos.**

- ✅ Use subfolders to organize functions (e.g., `authfn/python/`, `authfn/ts-sdk/`)
- ❌ Do NOT create nested monorepos (e.g., `authfn/` should NOT be another monorepo)
- ✅ Use Turbo workspaces defined in root `package.json`

Current workspaces:

```json
{
  "workspaces": [
    "searchfn",
    "botfn/*",
    "hostfn/*",
    "authfn/*",
    "packages/*",
    "21n/*"
  ]
}
```

### Rule D: Artifact Location

**Create artifacts (`.md` files) in `.conduct` folders**

- **Function-specific artifacts**: `{function}/.conduct/`
  - Examples: `authfn/.conduct/implementation.md`, `drawfn/.conduct/audit_report.md`
- **Shared/root artifacts**: `_conduct/`
  - Examples: `_conduct/implementation.md`, `_conduct/spec.md`

Artifact types:

- `implementation.md` - Implementation plans
- `spec.md` - Technical specifications
- `audit_report.md` - Code audits and reviews
- `task.md` - Task tracking
- `walkthrough.md` - Feature walkthroughs

## 🗂️ Language Support

Most core functions support **both TypeScript and Python**:

### TypeScript Structure

```
{function}/
├── typescript/       or  core/
│   ├── src/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── tsconfig.json
│   └── vitest.config.ts
```

### Python Structure

```
{function}/
├── python/
│   ├── {function}/        # Python package directory
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── tests/
│   ├── pyproject.toml
│   └── README.md
```

### Examples

- `authfn/typescript/` + `authfn/python/`
- `cachefn/typescript/` + `cachefn/python/`
- `secfn/typescript/` + `secfn/python/`
- `plugfn/core/` + `plugfn/python/`
- `drawfn/core/` (TypeScript only, with React/Svelte adapters)
- `searchfn/` (TypeScript only, browser-focused)

## 🔧 Development Workflow

### Building

```bash
# Build all packages
npm run build

# Build specific package (from root)
turbo run build --filter=authfn
turbo run build --filter=@superfunctions/db

# Build from package directory
cd authfn/ts-sdk && npm run build
```

### Testing

```bash
# Test all packages
npm test

# Test specific package
turbo run test --filter=drawfn

# Watch mode
npm run test:watch
```

### Linting

```bash
npm run lint
```

### Package Manager

- **npm** (v10.2.0+) - Specified in `packageManager` field
- Uses npm workspaces for monorepo management
- Turbo for build orchestration

## 🎯 Key Superfunctions Features

### AuthFn

- Multi-provider authentication (OAuth, API keys, JWT)
- Framework-agnostic with adapters for Express, Fastify, Hono, Next.js, SvelteKit
- Database-agnostic (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- TypeScript + Python SDKs

### DrawFn

- Cross-framework drawing canvas
- React and Svelte adapters
- Scene management, export capabilities
- Tolerant parsing with version validation

### PlugFn

- Self-hosted integration platform
- 75+ provider integrations (GitHub, Slack, Discord, Linear, Stripe)
- OAuth 2.0 flow handling
- Webhook support
- Multi-tenant with secure token storage

### SearchFn

- Browser-first full-text search
- IndexedDB persistence with in-memory LRU cache
- BM25 scoring
- FlexSearch-compatible API
- Worker-ready with snapshot export/import

### MailFn

- Stable and expiring programmable inboxes
- Cloudflare Email Workers, D1, R2, and Queues deployment adapter
- Raw MIME and attachment evidence, waits, OTP/link extraction, threads, labels, and search
- Typed client, test helpers, CLI, MCP server, custom domains, webhooks, and SendFn composition
- Scoped credentials, retention, audit, quotas, and explicitly gated public-platform controls

### CacheFn

- Multi-tier caching (memory, IndexedDB, external)
- Function memoization
- TTL and invalidation strategies
- Browser and server support

### SecFn

- Secrets vault management
- Access control and permissions
- Rate limiting
- Security monitoring
- Secret scanning

### BotFn

- Multi-platform bot framework
- Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations
- Shared types and persistence layer
- Event-driven architecture

## 🛠️ Common Tasks

### Adding a New Function

1. Create top-level directory: `{functionname}/`
2. Add TypeScript SDK: `{functionname}/typescript/` or `{functionname}/ts-sdk/`
3. (Optional) Add Python SDK: `{functionname}/python/`
4. Create `.conduct/` for artifacts
5. Add to workspace in root `package.json`
6. Package name: `{functionname}` (not scoped unless multi-package)

### Adding a Shared Package

1. Create in `packages/{name}/`
2. Package name: `@superfunctions/{name}`
3. Add to workspace (already covered by `packages/*`)
4. Update dependent packages

### Creating Artifacts

1. Function-specific: `{function}/.conduct/{artifact}.md`
2. Shared/root: `_conduct/{artifact}.md`
3. Use consistent naming: `implementation.md`, `spec.md`, `audit_report.md`, etc.

### Working with Turbo

```bash
# Run task across all packages
turbo run build
turbo run test

# Run for specific package
turbo run build --filter=authfn

# Run with dependencies
turbo run build --filter=authfn...

# Clear cache
turbo run clean
```

## 📚 Important Files

### Root Configuration

- `package.json` - Workspace and script definitions
- `turbo.json` - Turbo build configuration
- `tsconfig.json` - TypeScript base config (if exists)

### Package Configuration

- `package.json` - Package metadata, dependencies, scripts
- `tsconfig.json` - TypeScript configuration
- `vitest.config.ts` - Test configuration
- `pyproject.toml` - Python package configuration

### Documentation

- `README.md` - Package overview and usage
- `SPEC.md` - Technical specification (common in larger functions)
- `.conduct/*.md` - Implementation plans, audits, tasks

## 🔍 Finding Code

### Search Patterns

- **Function implementations**: `{function}/typescript/src/` or `{function}/python/{function}/`
- **Tests**: `__tests__/`, `tests/`, `*.test.ts`, `test_*.py`
- **Types**: `types.ts`, `models.py`, `src/types/`
- **Adapters**: `packages/http-*/`, `packages/python-*/`, `adapters/`
- **Examples**: `examples/`, `{function}/examples/`

### Key Directories

```
superfunctions/
├── {function}/              # Core function packages
│   ├── typescript/          # TS implementation
│   ├── python/              # Python implementation
│   ├── .conduct/            # Artifacts
│   ├── README.md            # Documentation
│   └── SPEC.md              # Specification (if exists)
├── packages/                # Shared packages
│   ├── {name}/              # @superfunctions/{name}
│   └── python-{name}/       # Python shared packages
└── _conduct/                # Root artifacts
```

## 🚀 Best Practices

### Super functions ecosystem (Very important)

- Reuse shared packages from `packages/` folder like http abstraction, db abstraction, etc.
- Never duplicate shared code like http adapters, db abstractions, etc.
- Don't reexport http-adapters etc - end consumers of the core function package will use the adapters directly. Refer `authfn` implementation for usage of core http router, core db, http adapters and db interface usage.
- Function packages that accept a `@superfunctions/db` `Adapter` must wrap the incoming adapter internally with their own schema, for example `wrapWithSchema(config.database, getSchema(...))`, before passing it to services/storage. Do not require app consumers to pass `adapterSchema` to `drizzleAdapter`, `kyselyAdapter`, `prismaAdapter`, or `memoryAdapter`; `adapterSchema` is a deprecated compatibility escape hatch for direct app-level adapter use.

### Code Organization

- Keep shared code in `packages/`
- Keep function-specific code in `{function}/`
- Use TypeScript for type safety
- Provide Python SDKs for backend-focused functions
- Write comprehensive tests

### Documentation

- Update README.md with usage examples
- Create SPEC.md for complex functions
- Document breaking changes
- Keep artifacts in `.conduct/` folders

### Testing

- Use Vitest for TypeScript
- Use pytest for Python
- Maintain high test coverage
- Test adapters separately

### Versioning

- Follow semantic versioning
- Coordinate versions across language SDKs
- Document migration guides for breaking changes

## 🔗 Related Resources

- **Repository**: https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions
- **License**: MIT (most packages) / Apache-2.0 (some packages)
- **Organization**: 21n
- **Contact**: hello@21n.org

## 📝 Notes for AI Agents

1. **Always check both TypeScript and Python** implementations when working on core functions
2. **Respect the naming conventions** - shared packages use `@superfunctions/`, functions use simple names
3. **Create artifacts in `.conduct/` folders**, not in root or arbitrary locations
4. **Avoid nested monorepos** - use subfolders within the main Turbo monorepo
5. **Use Turbo commands** for cross-package operations
6. **Check existing patterns** in similar functions before implementing new features
7. **Maintain consistency** across TypeScript and Python SDKs
8. **Update workspaces** in root `package.json` when adding new packages
9. **Follow existing test patterns** (Vitest for TS, pytest for Python)
10. **Document thoroughly** - this is a developer-focused ecosystem

---

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-10
**Monorepo Version**: 0.1.0
**Package Manager**: npm@10.2.0
**Build Tool**: Turbo v2.0.0

{"cmd":"cat > catchfn/.conduct/event-index-readiness.md <<'EOF'
# Canonical indexed Watch storage

The Catch branch now includes WatchFn's schema-owned event projections, required type/app/time and type/app/severity indexes, issue/session/replay indexes, conservative query pushdown and bounded offline backfill. This closes the missing canonical index implementation from the original Persistence & Storage section without adding a separate report service or transport. The full payload remains authoritative, and BotFn intake/link writes maintain projections atomically with the canonical event.

Existing deployments must apply the additive Watch schema migration before starting new writers. Historical null/unknown projection versions remain visible through a compatibility scan until offline backfill completes. Stop writers, workers and queries during backfill; follow its storage-ID cursor until null. Projection version 1 is an internal completeness invariant, not a field for application writers to set independently. Read the [migration contract, SQLite DDL and limitations](../../watchfn/.conduct/event-index-readiness.md).

The three Catch acceptance scripts now create numeric epoch columns and every declared index. The actual loopback HTTP/SQLite script checks the projection values from built Catch ingestion, combines type/app/severity/session and exact time-range filters, and repeats filtered retrieval after closing/reopening SQLite. Its authentication, retries, ambiguous-response at-least-once behavior and storage-failure assertions remain intact. The actual Chrome/BotFn script covers delayed verified issue links, cancellation, errors and SQLite reopen; the cross-origin browser delivery script covers CORS and transport behavior against the same indexed schema.

Validation: all 103 Catch SDK tests, TypeScript checks and CJS/ESM/declaration builds pass. The HTTP/SQLite, Chrome/BotFn and cross-origin Chrome acceptance commands pass. These runs use the freshly built Watch core from the identical merged source in the sibling Watch checkout via `CATCHFN_WATCH_CORE`; the Catch checkout's scoped install still lacks the optional adapter packages needed for Watch's complete multi-entry build. No dependency/lock changes or provider messages were needed.

Watch's own new native scenario migrates an old two-column SQLite table with 1005 rows, proves old reports remain queryable before backfill, verifies bounded/idempotent traversal and unchanged payload bytes, reopens the file, and confirms SQLite selects the type/app/time index. Its 179 core tests, types/build, and actual BotFn HTTP/native regressions also pass; details are recorded with the Watch change.

## Scope clarification and remaining requirements

The original Catch specification explicitly says “Future: Python SDK to open bug reports from backend contexts.” Therefore canonical Python client parity is deferred work, not an unmet v1 deliverable. The existing Python package remains a separate flat-report server, and its historical Python 3.8 compatibility claim remains unresolved against shared dependencies requiring 3.10. It is not evidence of canonical Watch delivery.

Retention defaults/bug-specific TTL, scalable broad queries and tag/aggregation execution, hosted provider/database validation, migration operations and deployment remain open. The supplied upload callback implements the original provided-endpoint alternative for large attachments; Watch does not currently provide a file channel, and this change does not invent one. Indexes do not establish tenant isolation or production readiness. Existing Watch API-key authority and trusted-application limits continue to apply.

# Canonical bug-report TTL acceptance

Catch's canonical Watch storage now implements the original v1 retention requirement: configured reports inherit Watch's 30-day retention default, with a server-owned bug-report TTL override. This does not modify the separate flat-report service or introduce a new browser/Python transport.

Hosts configure a fixed app allowlist and TTL policy on Watch, apply the nullable `receivedAt` schema migration, and schedule bounded `cleanupRetention` passes. The clock is the application host's `Date.now()`, not client event time or the database server clock; ingest and cleanup hosts need synchronized clocks. Historical reports remain protected until an explicit offline migration-anchor backfill. See [the complete policy, migration and failure contract](../../watchfn/.conduct/event-retention-readiness.md).

Unresolved issue deliveries are protected beyond TTL. Only linked canonical payloads may expire; their outbox receipts and content fingerprints remain indefinitely. Exact replays remain acknowledged without resurrecting a payload or creating another provider issue. Conflicting replays still fail, and authenticated status remains available to Catch polling. Removing receipt history or changing namespaces would break that guarantee and is outside this payload-retention operation.

The actual built SDK/Chrome acceptance script now enables a short fixture-only bug TTL but schedules cleanup only after existing widget/delivery checks. It traverses six linked reports in two-row cleanup pages, proves a second pass deletes nothing, replays the original accepted HTTP envelope without a new provider create or payload, closes/reopens SQLite, and calls built Catch's `pollIssueStatus` against the actual mounted Watch endpoint. The verified issue link remains available while all six payloads are absent and six receipt records remain. Existing lost-ack deduplication, authorization/route rejection, real Chrome widget polling/cancellation and provider protocol checks still pass.

The canonical HTTP/SQLite and cross-origin Chrome acceptance scripts also pass against the new schema with retention unconfigured, preserving existing at-least-once behavior. Source tests/types/build remain unchanged by this Catch script/documentation checkpoint. Watch's 188 source tests, type/build checks, three native BotFn scenarios, and 1005-row historical migration/arrival initialization pass. Tests use the freshly built Watch core from the identical merged source in the sibling checkout via `CATCHFN_WATCH_CORE`; no hosted provider issue or message is created.

# AGENTS.md - AI Agent Development Guide for Superfunctions

> **Purpose**: This document provides AI agents with essential information for working effectively on the Superfunctions monorepo.

## 🏗️ Repository Structure

Superfunctions is a **Turbo monorepo** containing self-hosted developer tools and libraries. The repository is organized into:

### Core Functions (Top-Level Directories)

Individual superfunction packages, each providing specific developer capabilities:

- **`authfn/`** - Authentication & API key management
- **`cachefn/`** - Multi-tier caching with function memoization
- **`drawfn/`** - Cross-framework drawing canvas for brainstorming
- **`plugfn/`** - Integration platform (OAuth, webhooks, 75+ providers)
- **`searchfn/`** - Browser-first full-text search with IndexedDB
- **`secfn/`** - Security functions (secrets vault, rate limiting, monitoring)
- **`testfn/`** - Testing utilities and frameworks
- **`botfn/`** - Bot framework (Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations)
- **`hostfn/`** - Hosting and deployment utilities
- **`uifn/`** - UI components and utilities
- **`watchfn/`** - File watching and monitoring
- **`billfn/`** - Billing and payment processing
- **`browsefn/`** - Browser automation utilities
- **`chartfn/`** - Charting and visualization
- **`datafn/`** - Data processing utilities
- **`docsfn/`** - Documentation generation
- **`filefn/`** - File operations and management
- **`flowfn/`** - Flow control (queues, streams, workflows)
- **`iconfn/`** - Icon utilities
- **`logfn/`** - Logging utilities
- **`mailfn/`** - Programmable real inboxes for products, agents, and tests
- **`sendfn/`** - Email/messaging utilities

### Shared Packages (`packages/`)

Framework-agnostic core libraries used across superfunctions:

**TypeScript Packages:**

- `@superfunctions/http` - HTTP abstractions
- `@superfunctions/http-express` - Express.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-fastify` - Fastify adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-hono` - Hono adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-next` - Next.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-sveltekit` - SvelteKit adapter
- `@superfunctions/db` - Database adapter system (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- `@superfunctions/auth` - Authentication abstraction layer
- `@superfunctions/cli` - CLI tool for schema management

**Python Packages:**

- `superfunctions` (from `python-core/`) - Core namespace package
- `superfunctions-sqlalchemy` (from `python-sqlalchemy/`)
- `superfunctions-fastapi` (from `python-fastapi/`)
- `superfunctions-flask` (from `python-flask/`)

### Other Directories

- **`_conduct/`** - Root-level artifacts for shared code (implementation plans, specs, audits)
- **`21n/`** - Organization-specific packages
- **`.agent/`** - Agent workflows and automation
- **`.github/`** - GitHub Actions and CI/CD

## 📦 Package Naming Conventions

### Rule A: Shared Packages Format

**Any package shared across superfunctions uses `@superfunctions/{name}` format**

Examples:

```
packages/db/          → @superfunctions/db
packages/http/        → @superfunctions/http
packages/auth/        → @superfunctions/auth
packages/cli/         → @superfunctions/cli
```

### Rule B: Core Function Packages Format

**Single-package functions**: Use simple name without scope

```
authfn/ts-sdk/        → authfn
drawfn/core/          → drawfn
cachefn/typescript/   → cachefn
plugfn/core/         → plugfn
searchfn/             → searchfn
```

**Multi-package functions**: Use `@{functionname}/{sub-package}` format (if needed in future)

```
@authfn/core          (example for future multi-package structure)
@authfn/providers     (example for future multi-package structure)
```

**Current Status**: All core functions currently use single-package structure. The scoped format is reserved for future expansion if a function needs multiple published packages.

### Rule C: Monorepo Structure

**The root `superfunctions` is a Turbo monorepo. Avoid nested monorepos.**

- ✅ Use subfolders to organize functions (e.g., `authfn/python/`, `authfn/ts-sdk/`)
- ❌ Do NOT create nested monorepos (e.g., `authfn/` should NOT be another monorepo)
- ✅ Use Turbo workspaces defined in root `package.json`

Current workspaces:

```json
{
  "workspaces": [
    "searchfn",
    "botfn/*",
    "hostfn/*",
    "authfn/*",
    "packages/*",
    "21n/*"
  ]
}
```

### Rule D: Artifact Location

**Create artifacts (`.md` files) in `.conduct` folders**

- **Function-specific artifacts**: `{function}/.conduct/`
  - Examples: `authfn/.conduct/implementation.md`, `drawfn/.conduct/audit_report.md`
- **Shared/root artifacts**: `_conduct/`
  - Examples: `_conduct/implementation.md`, `_conduct/spec.md`

Artifact types:

- `implementation.md` - Implementation plans
- `spec.md` - Technical specifications
- `audit_report.md` - Code audits and reviews
- `task.md` - Task tracking
- `walkthrough.md` - Feature walkthroughs

## 🗂️ Language Support

Most core functions support **both TypeScript and Python**:

### TypeScript Structure

```
{function}/
├── typescript/       or  core/
│   ├── src/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── tsconfig.json
│   └── vitest.config.ts
```

### Python Structure

```
{function}/
├── python/
│   ├── {function}/        # Python package directory
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── tests/
│   ├── pyproject.toml
│   └── README.md
```

### Examples

- `authfn/typescript/` + `authfn/python/`
- `cachefn/typescript/` + `cachefn/python/`
- `secfn/typescript/` + `secfn/python/`
- `plugfn/core/` + `plugfn/python/`
- `drawfn/core/` (TypeScript only, with React/Svelte adapters)
- `searchfn/` (TypeScript only, browser-focused)

### Building

```bash
# Build all packages
npm run build

# Build specific package (from root)
turbo run build --filter=authfn
turbo run build --filter=@superfunctions/db

# Build from package directory
cd authfn/ts-sdk && npm run build
```

### Testing

```bash
# Test all packages
npm test

# Test specific package
turbo run test --filter=drawfn

# Watch mode
npm run test:watch
```

### Linting

```bash
npm run lint
```

### Package Manager

- **npm** (v10.2.0+) - Specified in `packageManager` field
- Uses npm workspaces for monorepo management
- Turbo for build orchestration

## 🎯 Key Superfunctions Features

### AuthFn

- Multi-provider authentication (OAuth, API keys, JWT)
- Framework-agnostic with adapters for Express, Fastify, Hono, Next.js, SvelteKit
- Database-agnostic (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- TypeScript + Python SDKs

- React and Svelte adapters
- Scene management, export capabilities

- Webhook support
- Multi-tenant with secure token storage

- Browser-first full-text search
- IndexedDB persistence with in-memory LRU cache
- BM25 scoring
- FlexSearch-compatible API
- Worker-ready with snapshot export/import

- Stable and expiring programmable inboxes
- Cloudflare Email Workers, D1, R2, and Queues deployment adapter
- Raw MIME and attachment evidence, waits, OTP/link extraction, threads, labels, and search
- Typed client, test helpers, CLI, MCP server, custom domains, webhooks, and SendFn composition

- Multi-tier caching (memory, IndexedDB, external)
- Function memoization
- TTL and invalidation strategies
- Browser and server support

### SecFn

- Secrets vault management
- Access control and permissions
- Rate limiting
- Security monitoring
- Secret scanning

### BotFn

- Multi-platform bot framework
- Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations
- Shared types and persistence layer
- Event-driven architecture

## 🛠️ Common Tasks

### Adding a New Function

1. Create top-level directory: `{functionname}/`
2. Add TypeScript SDK: `{functionname}/typescript/` or `{functionname}/ts-sdk/`
3. (Optional) Add Python SDK: `{functionname}/python/`
4. Create `.conduct/` for artifacts
5. Add to workspace in root `package.json`
6. Package name: `{functionname}` (not scoped unless multi-package)

### Adding a Shared Package

1. Create in `packages/{name}/`
2. Package name: `@superfunctions/{name}`
3. Add to workspace (already covered by `packages/*`)
4. Update dependent packages

### Creating Artifacts

1. Function-specific: `{function}/.conduct/{artifact}.md`
2. Shared/root: `_conduct/{artifact}.md`
3. Use consistent naming: `implementation.md`, `spec.md`, `audit_report.md`, etc.

### Working with Turbo

```bash
# Run task across all packages
turbo run build
turbo run test

# Run for specific package
turbo run build --filter=authfn

# Run with dependencies
turbo run build --filter=authfn...

## 🚀 Best Practices

### Super functions ecosystem (Very important)

- Reuse shared packages from `packages/` folder like http abstraction, db abstraction, etc.
- Never duplicate shared code like http adapters, db abstractions, etc.
- Don't reexport http-adapters etc - end consumers of the core function package will use the adapters directly. Refer `authfn` implementation for usage of core http router, core db, http adapters and db interface usage.
- Function packages that accept a `@superfunctions/db` `Adapter` must wrap the incoming adapter internally with their own schema, for example `wrapWithSchema(config.database, getSchema(...))`, before passing it to services/storage. Do not require app consumers to pass `adapterSchema` to `drizzleAdapter`, `kyselyAdapter`, `prismaAdapter`, or `memoryAdapter`; `adapterSchema` is a deprecated compatibility escape hatch for direct app-level adapter use.

### Code Organization

- Keep shared code in `packages/`
- Keep function-specific code in `{function}/`
- Use TypeScript for type safety
